title: How to Run
text:
This will be a fast guide on how to run the federeated environment step by step.

1 What do you need
In order to make everything work properly you shuold: - Install R - Install Docker - Download for our GitHub repo (https://github.com/FAIRVASC/federated/main) the Federated_Learning directory

SQLSPARQL



1.0.1 Step 1
Open your shell, move into the Federated_Learning directory and create the password for the user-master communication and for the master-slave communication
export FAIRVASC_APP_PASSWORD='fairvasc'
export FAIRVASC_WORKER_PASSWORD='worker'


1.0.2 Step 2
Run setup.sh
sh setup.sh SQL


1.0.3 Step 3
Run DataPreparation.R
Rscript DataPreparation.R


1.0.4 Step 4
Create or Check your /.Renviron file in order to have here the same password for the user you choose during step 1


1.0.5 Step 5
Run your script.R file using your favorite IDE


1.0.6 Step 6
Enjoy your Fairvasc SQL Federeated Environment
fv_run_model('SQL', 'Linear', 'quality', FEATURE_COLS)




1.0.7 Step 1
Run DataPreparation.R up to line 70
head -n 70 DataPreparation.R | Rscript -


1.0.8 Step 2
Run setup.sh
sh setup.sh SQL


1.0.9 Step 3
Run your script.R file using your favorite IDE


1.0.10 Step 4
Enjoy your Fairvasc SPARQL Federeated Environment
fv_run_model('SPARQL', 'Linear', 'quality', FEATURE_COLS)

title: Tabset
text:
4.2 Slave to Master
For each time t contained in the global_times array, the Slave returns a JSON object containing exclusively these 5 aggregated metrics:
S0 (Scalar): Anonymous sum of risks.
S1 (Vector): Anonymous sum of covariates multiplied by the risk.
S2 (Matrix): Anonymous sum of the cross-products of covariates multiplied by the risk.
count_events (Integer): How many people in the Slave experienced the event at exactly time t.
event_sum (Vector): The mathematical sum of the covariates (X values) of the patients who experienced the event at time t.

title: Cox Proportional Hazard Model
text:
The algorithm implements a Federated Cox Proportional Hazards model using the Newton-Raphson optimization method to maximize the partial likelihood. Unlike standard linear or Poisson regression, the Cox model requires evaluating the risk set at specific event times across the entire dataset. To achieve this in a federated architecture, the algorithm is split into two distinct phases:

Phase 1: Event Time Discovery: Before optimization begins, the global set of unique event times must be identified. Each slave node scans its local data to find the distinct times where an event occurred (ignoring right-censored observations). The master aggregates these local times, removes duplicates, and creates a globally sorted array of event times.
Phase 2: Newton-Raphson Optimization: Using the global event times, the master initiates an iterative loop. Given the current global parameter vector \(\beta^{(t)}\):
Local Computation (Slave Node): Each slave computes the linear predictor \(\eta_i\) and local risk \(\exp(\eta_i)\). For every global event time \(t\), the slave calculates the partial derivatives of the partial likelihood: \(S^{(0)}\) (sum of risk), \(S^{(1)}\) (risk-weighted predictors), and \(S^{(2)}\) (risk-weighted covariance) for all patients still at risk (\(d.t \geq t\)). It also tallies the predictor values (event_sum) for patients experiencing an event at exactly time \(t\).
Global Aggregation & Update (Master Node): The master aggregates the \(S^{(0)}\), \(S^{(1)}\), and \(S^{(2)}\) components across all slaves for each time \(t\). Using these global statistics, it computes the gradient vector (\(U\)) and the information/Hessian matrix (\(I\)). Finally, it computes the update step (delta) via matrix inversion: \(\delta = I^{-1} U\), and updates the parameters.

3.2 Slave to Master
The slaves sand informational data to the master two times: - Phase 1 : JSON arrays containing the unique local survival times when the event of interest occurred. - Phase 2 : Iterativly for each global timepoint slaves send structured vectors or JSON objects containing, for each time point: the time being examined (time), the sum at risk (S0), the vector (S1), the matrix (S2), the sum of covariates for those who experienced the event (event_sum), and the total number of events that occurred (count_events).

title: Multivariate Linear Model
text:
The algorithm implements a distributed Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression. Each slave node computes locally:
\[X_{k}^TX_{k}\]
and
\[X_{k}^Ty_{k}.\]
The master node aggregates the local statistics:
\[X^TX=\sum_{k}X_{k}^TX_{k}\]
\[X^Ty=\sum_{k}X_{k}^Ty_{k}\]
The master estimates the global regression coefficients:
\[\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty\]
The slave nodes compute their local RSS (Residual Sum of Squares) using the global estimate \(\beta\). The master computes: residual variance, standard errors, t-statistics. The main advantage of this approach is that raw data never leaves the local nodes; only aggregated sufficient statistics are exchanged.

title: Multivariate Linear Model
text:
3.2 Slave to Master
Each Slave computes local sufficient statistics and returns a JSON payload containing:

XTX (\(X_k^T X_k\)): Local cross-product matrix of predictors.
XTY (\(X_k^T y_k\)): Local vector product of predictors and the target variable.
n: Number of valid local observations (excluding NaN targets).
ysum (\(\sum y_{k}\)): Sum of local target values.
yty (\(\sum y_{k}^2\)): Sum of local squared target values.

title: Data Simulation
text:
Last step of the initialization is to create our databases inside our two slaves.
We are using 2 test dataset for testing purposes: a. winequality for most of the prediction model; b. bladder for our risk analysis
Remember to always run this first in order to produce the .ttl files before your SPARQL environment creation


Code
# =============================================================
# DATA PREPARATION - Prediction model
# =============================================================
setwd("~/Desktop/Federated_Learning/")
winequality <- read.csv("http://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/wine-quality/winequality-white.csv", sep = ";")
winequality$binary_quality <- ifelse(winequality$quality >= 6, 1, 0)
colnames(winequality) <- gsub("\\.", "_", colnames(winequality))
colnames(winequality)<- tolower(colnames(winequality))

set.seed(123)
slave1_data <- winequality[sample.int(nrow(winequality), 123), ]
set.seed(321)
slave2_data <- winequality[sample.int(nrow(winequality), 321), ]
all_data <- rbind(slave1_data, slave2_data)

# convert into .ttl
library(readr)
csv_to_turtle <- function(table, output_path, slave_id) {
  df <- table
  feature_cols <- names(df)[1:11]
  y_col        <- "quality"
  
  
  lines <- c('@prefix fv: <http://example.org/fairvasc#> .\n')
  
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(df))) {
    
    uri      <- sprintf("<http://example.org/patient/%s/%04d>", slave_id, i)
    features <- paste(as.numeric(df[i, feature_cols]), collapse = " ")
    y_val    <- as.numeric(df[i, y_col])
    
    lines <- c(lines,
               sprintf('%s fv:features "%s" ;', uri, features),
               sprintf('   fv:y        "%g"  .\n', y_val)
    )
  }
  writeLines(lines, output_path)
  cat(sprintf("Written: %s  (%d rows)\n", output_path, nrow(df)))
}

csv_to_turtle(slave1_data, 'slave1.ttl', 'slave1')
csv_to_turtle(slave2_data, 'slave2.ttl', 'slave2')

# =============================================================
# DATA PREPARATION - Risk model
# =============================================================
library(survival)

bladder <- survival::bladder
bladder$treatment <- bladder$rx - 1
cox_slave1_data <- bladder[1:200, c("treatment","number","size","stop","event")]
cox_slave2_data <- bladder[201:340, c("treatment","number","size","stop","event")]
cox_all_data <- bladder

cox_to_turtle <- function(df, output_path) {
  lines <- c('@prefix : <http://example.org/> .',
             '@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .')
  
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(df))) {
    lines <- c(lines,
               sprintf(':p%d :treatment %d ; :number %d ; :size %d ; :stop %d ; :event %d .',
                       i, df$treatment[i], df$number[i], df$size[i], df$stop[i], df$event[i]))
  }
  writeLines(lines, output_path)
  cat(sprintf("Written: %s  (%d rows)\n", output_path, nrow(df)))
}

cox_to_turtle(cox_slave1_data, 'cox_slave1.ttl')
cox_to_turtle(cox_slave2_data, 'cox_slave2.ttl')

title: Poisson Regression
text:
The algorithm implements a Federated Poisson Regression using the Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) optimization method. Poisson regression is standard for modeling count data and relies on a log-link function.
The theoretical model assumes the expected value of the response variable \(y_i\) given predictors \(x_i\) is:
\[\mu_i = E(y_i | x_i) = \exp(x_i^T \beta)\]
To estimate the parameter vector \(\beta\) iteratively in a federated architecture, the computation is split:

Local Computation (Slave Node): Given the current global parameter vector \(\beta^{(t)}\), each slave \(k\) calculates the linear predictor \(\eta_i = x_i^T \beta^{(t)}\) and the expected rate \(\mu_i = \exp(\eta_i)\). The iterative formulation requires a working weight \(w_i = \mu_i\) and an adjusted dependent variable \(z_i = \eta_i + \frac{y_i - \mu_i}{\mu_i}\). The slave then computes its local components for the normal equations: the weighted cross-product matrix \(X_k^T W_k X_k\) and the weighted vector product \(X_k^T W_k z_k\).
Global Aggregation & Update (Master Node): The master aggregates the local components to reconstruct the global matrices: \[X^T W X = \sum_k X_k^T W_k X_k, \quad X^T W z = \sum_k X_k^T W_k z_k\] To prevent singular Hessian matrices, a ridge penalty (\(\lambda = 10^{-6}\)) is added to the diagonal of \(X^T W X\). The master calculates the raw parameter update \(\beta_{new} = (X^T W X)^{-1} (X^T W z)\). To ensure stability across iterations, a damping factor/learning rate (\(\alpha = 0.3\)) is applied to smooth the update: \(\beta^{(t+1)} = \alpha \beta_{new} + (1 - \alpha) \beta^{(t)}\).

title: Naive Logistic Regression
text:
The algorithm implements an iterative Federated Logistic Regression using the Newton-Raphson optimization method (Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares). Because logistic regression lacks a closed-form solution, the model requires iterative updates until convergence.
The probability model for binary classification is defined as:
\[\mu_i = P(y_i = 1 | x_i) = \sigma(z_i) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z_i}}, \quad z_i = x_i^T \beta\]
The global Log-Likelihood (\(LL\)) maximized by the model is:
\[LL(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i \ln(\mu_i) + (1 - y_i) \ln(1 - \mu_i) \right]\]
In a federated architecture, the computation is distributed as follows:

Local Computation (Slave Node): Given the current global parameter vector \(\beta^{(t)}\), each slave \(k\) evaluates predicted probabilities \(\mu_i\) for its local observations. To avoid numerical instability (such as \(\ln(0)\)), predictions are clamped to the range \([\epsilon, 1-\epsilon]\) with \(\epsilon = 10^{-15}\). Each slave computes:

Local Log-Likelihood (\(LL_k\))
Local Gradient vector \(G_k = X_k^T (y_k - \mu_k)\)
Local Hessian matrix \(H_k = X_k^T W_k X_k\), where \(W_k = \text{diag}(\mu_i (1 - \mu_i))\)

Global Aggregation & Update (Master Node): The master aggregates summary statistics across all nodes:
\[H = \sum_k H_k, \quad G = \sum_k G_k, \quad LL = \sum_k LL_k\]
To handle potential matrix singularity when weights collapse toward zero, a ridge regularization parameter (\(\lambda = 10^{-6}\)) is added to the diagonal of \(H\).
The raw Newton update step is computed as:
\[\text{raw\_delta} = H^{-1} G\]
A learning rate / damping factor (\(\alpha = 0.3\)) is applied to stabilize updates:
\[\Delta = \alpha \cdot \text{raw\_delta}\]
The parameter vector is updated as \(\beta^{(t+1)} = \beta^{(t)} + \Delta\). The process repeats until the maximum coefficient change falls below the tolerance (\(\max |\Delta_i| < 10^{-6}\)) or maximum iterations are reached.

3.1 Master to Slave
The Master sends this to the Slave:
Database metadata: Table name and column names (tbl_name, y_col, x_cols); beta: The current global parameter vector \(\beta^t\). This vector is required by slaves to update predictions \(\mu_i\), observation weights \(w_i\), gradient \(G_k\), and Hessian \(H_k\).

title: Security
text:
One of the main aspect of this whole approach is to ensure that the user may only interrogate the intermediary (master), and that he will only ask pre-approved questions. That said, we have to define a security layer that will force the user to this limitations since in our idea the main field of application of this technology would be the medical area, and we do care about patients privacy. Ideally no port outside the network should be open for the slaves (we have it in our test env just for semplicity), so the first of the two constraints is already included in our build since the only way the user have to interact with the network is through the master. In order to accomplish and test also the second we are going to define some security features.
IMPORTANT: From now on we will refer just to the SQL security features because in our knowledge SPARQL do not have any built-in privacy preserving feature. It is a language thought to enhance sharability thus in our simulation we are accepting as a limit that the SPARQL user is meant to just be aware of the limits and guidlines he is supposed to follow, and wont by any means try to overcome those limits.

title: Security
text:
2 SQL Security
In an SQL environment is possible to create and define different Users each with his personal characteristics. In this framework we are mainly using two different users:

The first one is the super user ‘fairvasc_app’, a specific user with limited amount of permits that we will define and control for the user-master communication; 
The second is the user ‘worker_user’, a specific user with limited amount of permits that we will define and control for the master-slave communication.

In the Docker Setup section you could have noticed a specific command during the slave creation:
echo "▸ Creating restricted application role on master (fairvasc_app)..."
  docker exec master psql -U postgres -c "CREATE ROLE fairvasc_app WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '$FAIRVASC_APP_PASSWORD' NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;"
This is defining in mastervour safe user that will have the right to perform calculus and have acces to all the function we are going to implement in the system. The NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE is a specification that basically negates every power besides the one that we are explicitly giving to the role.
We can do the same in the slaves for the master-slave communication:
docker exec slave$i psql -U postgres -c "CREATE ROLE worker_user WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '$FAIRVASC_WORKER_PASSWORD' NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;"

title: Univariate Linear Model
Setup
text:
1 Introduction
Through this page you will find a guide for this ready to use SQL Federated Learning (FL) simulation. The aim is to help you to create from scratch an environment in which isolated containers (slave/registries) can be interrogated by authorized users via a ‘super’ container (master/web interface). We are using a single bash script as setup filef or both the SQL and SPARQL environments. All the container aspect is handled using docker.


2 Building the network
Let’s start delving into our setup file. For this example we will have 1 ‘super’ container (master) and two registries (slave1 and slave2). First of all we need to define if we are going to work in SQL or SPARQL:
#!/bin/bash
set -e

FRAMEWORK=$1
NETWORK_NAME="Fairvasc"

if [ -z "$FRAMEWORK" ]; then
  echo " Error: Please specify the framework."
  echo "Usage: sh setup.sh SQL   -or-   sh setup.sh SPARQL"
  exit 1
fi
FRAMEWORK: the type of environment we want to build. For now we developed the code only for SQL and SPARQL, but if needed in the future new languages structure could be added; 
NETWORK_NAME: the name we are giving to our containers net. All containers joining the Network open a port for information exchange that can be reached only by the other Fairvasc-containers. 
Now we clean possible previously existing containers and build our empty containers network:

echo "▸ Cleaning up old containers..."
docker rm -f master slave1 slave2 2>/dev/null || true
docker network inspect $NETWORK_NAME >/dev/null 2>&1 || docker network create $NETWORK_NAME
Find attached specifics chunk of code for each of the available languages:

SQLSPARQL


Here you find the detailed code to build your SQL env.
if [ "$FRAMEWORK" = "SQL" ]; then
  echo -e "\n=== Booting SQL (PostgreSQL PL/v8) Environment ==="
  IMAGE="sibedge/postgres-plv8"
  docker pull $IMAGE

  docker run -d --name master --network $NETWORK_NAME -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=password $IMAGE
  until docker exec master pg_isready -U postgres >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done
  docker exec master psql -U postgres -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS plv8;"
  docker exec master psql -U postgres -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS dblink;"
  
  echo "▸ Creating restricted application role on master (fairvasc_app)..."
  docker exec master psql -U postgres -c "CREATE ROLE fairvasc_app WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '$FAIRVASC_APP_PASSWORD' NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;"


  for i in 1 2; do
    PORT=$((5432 + i))
    echo "▸ Starting Slave $i Node (Port $PORT)..."
    docker run -d --name slave$i --network $NETWORK_NAME -p $PORT:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=slv$i $IMAGE
    until docker exec slave$i pg_isready -U postgres >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done
    docker exec slave$i psql -U postgres -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS plv8;"
    docker exec slave$i psql -U postgres -c "CREATE ROLE worker_user WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '$FAIRVASC_WORKER_PASSWORD' NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;"
  done
  echo -e "\n SQL Network is ready!"
IMAGE: the docker image that will be used inside our containers (for semplicty we are using the same image for all the containers). A good image in our scope must have: 

postgres: our main SQL interpreter 
pl-v8: a ready to use postgres extension that allows to compile JavaScript code directly inside the postgres environment 

What this code is doing basically is creating our three containers starting on port 5432 (that is the standard one).
Besides some informational prints, this command is quite simple: 
docker run: basic comand used for starting a container; 
-d: it means detach, after the container creation, it will run in background leaving the terminal free to be interrogated again; 
–name: specify container name, in our case ‘master’; 
–network: through this command we are asking docker to add this container to our previously build network; 
-p: defines a port to access the container from outside the network. For the structure of our simulation, we will use R to reach this container, although is also possible to make use of this same code in an R-less environment using just the shell as interface fir the user; 
-e POSTGRES_PASSWORD: just uses our preferred master password as actual password of the container; 
$IMAGE: Import our IMAGE in the container. 
After that we just wait until everything is settled up and ready to use, so we can build our extensions. In detail we are creating two extensions: 

pl-v8: as specified before, it is our JavaScript compiler inside postgres 
dblink: a ready to use postgres extension that allows to the container to broadcast a query to other containers aiming to collect and retrieve their answers. 

The second one is required only for the master container, the slaves are supposed to be interrogated and not to interrogate, so they simply don’t need it.
Notice that for SQL both data and functions are not uploaded trough this setup in the containers. For simulated data visit the Data Simulation page, while for the functions inspect the page about the needed model


Here you find the detailed code to build your SPARQL env.

elif [ "$FRAMEWORK" = "SPARQL" ]; then
  echo -e "\n=== Booting SPARQL (Apache Jena Fuseki) Environment ==="
  FUSEKI_DIR="./fuseki-2.0"

  echo "▸ Bundling JavaScript files for Fuseki..."
  cat Federated_Network/utilities/*_master.js Federated_Network/SPARQL/*_master.js > fuseki_master_bundle.js 2>/dev/null || true
  cat Federated_Network/utilities/*_slave.js Federated_Network/SPARQL/*_slave.js > fuseki_slave_bundle.js 2>/dev/null || true

  echo "▸ Building Fuseki Image..."
  cd "$FUSEKI_DIR" && docker build -t fuseki . && cd ..

  start_fuseki() {
    docker run -d --name "$1" --network $NETWORK_NAME -p "$2:3030" -v "$(pwd)/$3:/jsfuncs.js" fuseki --update --set arq:js-library=/jsfuncs.js --mem /fv
  }

  start_fuseki master 3030 fuseki_master_bundle.js
  start_fuseki slave1 3031 fuseki_slave_bundle.js
  start_fuseki slave2 3032 fuseki_slave_bundle.js
  sleep 5

  echo "▸ Uploading TTL datasets to Slaves..."
  for i in 1 2; do
    if [ -f "slave${i}.ttl" ]; then
      curl -sf -X POST -H "Content-Type: text/turtle" --data-binary "@slave${i}.ttl" "http://localhost:303${i}/fv/data"
    fi
    if [ -f "cox_slave${i}.ttl" ]; then
      curl -sf -X POST -H "Content-Type: text/turtle" --data-binary "@cox_slave${i}.ttl" "http://localhost:303${i}/fv/data"
    fi
  done
  echo -e "\n SPARQL Network is ready!"
fi
FUSEKI_DIR: the directory in which our own docker image is stored.
Besides some informational prints, this command is quite simple: We create two files:

fuseki_master_bundle.js containing all functions needed in the master to make every model work;
fuseki_slave_bundle.js containing all functions needed in the slaves to make every model work.

We build our docker image and than through the start_fuseki() function we create our three containers: docker run: basic comand used for starting a container; 
-d: it means detach, after the container creation, it will run in background leaving the terminal free to be interrogated again; 
–name: specify container name, in our case ‘master’; 
–network: through this command we are asking docker to add this container to our previously build network; 
-p: defines a port to access the container from outside the network. For the structure of our simulation, we will use R to reach this container, although is also possible to make use of this same code in an R-less environment using just the shell as interface fir the user; 
-v “$(pwd)/$3:/jsfuncs.js”: $(pwd)/$3 gets the full path to a local file (where $3 is the filename or relative path you pass as the 3rd argument to start_fuseki); 
fuseki: name of the docker image to upload in the container;
–update: enable SPARQL Update: Allows read-write SPARQL operations (e.g., INSERT, DELETE) on the Fuseki server rather than making it read-only;
–set arq:js-library=/jsfuncs.js: registers the mounted JavaScript file (/jsfuncs.js) into Jena’s ARQ query engine so you can use custom JavaScript functions directly inside your SPARQL queries;
–mem: tells Fuseki to store the RDF dataset entirely in RAM instead of persisting it to the filesystem. (Data will be lost when the container stops).
/fv: dataset name
In the end we upload our prebuilt data (see Data Simulation) inside the slaves container.

title: Federated Learning in SQL/SPARQL + R
text:
FAIRVASC is a Europe-wide research project initiated by Prof. Mark Little (University of Dublin, Ireland) and Prof. Augusto Vaglio (University of Florence, Italy), funded by the European Joint Programme on Rare Diseases (EJPRD 2019). Its goal is to create Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable (FAIR) access to a network of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis (AAV) registries, enhancing research and care for AAV. The project has developed an infrastructure linking seven national/regional AAV registries into a single European dataset, providing a rich, reliable resource for ethical and secure research.
This infrastructure uses Semantic Web Technologies for privacy-compliant federated querying and semantic interoperability, enabling high-quality clinical research and federated learning for complex statistical modeling.
In FAIRVASC, this large new European resource will be analysed to identify features (clinical and physical characteristics, etc.) that predict how a patient’s illness will develop, and what their major health risks are. These markers can, in the future, be developed into new predictive tools that help doctors to choose the best treatment options for the individual patient.
Research into the rare condition – Vasculitis (an acquired, immune mediated inflammatory disease involving blood vessels of many tissues and organs), needs sufficiently large quantities of data to enable well-informed conclusions about treatments and possible cures. It is thus essential to combine the databases of patient registries of several countries to build a dataset of sufficient size to enable meaningful research.

2 AIM
To address the significant challenge of data siloing in RMD research, we will provide a reference FL registry environment with SPARQL backend in a reproducible containerised form. This will be open source and provided together with full supporting documentation to facilitate adoption and deployment by any consortia seeking to exploit these techniques, ensuring long-term and broad impact, not only on FAIRVASC. In parallel we will begin work on a standard SQL backend version, ensuring broad applicability for registries which may be based on more established technology. A proof-of-concept study utilising a sandbox semantic web environment and showcasing Simpson’s paradox for linear regression over distributed synthetic databases will be made available to demonstrate the environment.
